Abstract
#

Birkhoff and Pierce asked in 1956 whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible with the ring operations. Schwartz and Yang proved in 2011 that C\mathbb{C}C admits directed partial orders. We give a new construction that by using a transcendence basis of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q, we embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}}, so that every complex number acquires a series expansion, and we define positivity by a condition on the leading coefficient. Every directed partial order we construct is placed in a stratification by how much of the expansion a rule has to read. Reading one term, a window of fixed width, or a sensitivity condition on small changes, we obtain five nested conditions A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒EA \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow EA⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E and six types. Relative to the fixed level valuation, cones satisfying BBB correspond to the cards satisfying a product and a sum condition. Cones satisfying CCC are never lattice orders, which excludes Types 1, 2, 3. We give an example of Type 4 that is not a lattice order either. The existence of a lattice order on C\mathbb{C}C and the existence of orders of Types 5 and 6 still remain open. This is a stratification rather than a complete classification because only Types 1–4 are shown to be nonempty.

Keywords: directed partial order, cone, Puiseux series, valuation, lattice-ordered ring, Birkhoff–Pierce problem

1. Introduction
#

In 1956, Birkhoff and Pierce asked the question whether the complex field C\mathbb{C}C admits a lattice order compatible under the rings [1]; in 2011, Schwartz and Yang proved that the directed partial order are admitted on C\mathbb{C}C [2] and later found that a field admits one if and only if it has characteristic 0 and is real or has the transcendence degree at least 1 over Q\mathbb{Q}Q [3]. Furthermore, for a non-archimedean totally ordered field FFF, the directed partial orders on F(i)F(i)F(i) compatible with the order of FFF were studied and classified by Rump and Yang [4], Ma, Wu, and Zhang [5] [6] [7], and Xu and Zhang [8]. Recently, Wang, Yuan, Zhang, and Zhu [9] also give a related example by construction, stating the conjecture that there does not exist lattice order on the complex field. None of these orders is a lattice order. However, He [10] gives a certain answer that C\mathbb{C}C admits at least 2ℵ02^{\aleph_0}2ℵ0​ distinct compatible lattice orders.

This paper has two parts. The first part is a direct construction on C\mathbb{C}C as an abstract field without ordered subfield given in advance. We write C\mathbb{C}C as the algebraic closure of F(t)F(t)F(t), where ttt is transcendental and FFF is an algebraically closed subfield, put s=1/ts = 1/ts=1/t, and embed C\mathbb{C}C into the field of Puiseux series over FFF in sss. Thus, every complex number becomes a series like a decimal expansion. The second part constructs a stratification to sort all directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. We sort the orders by how much of the series must be read. With the restriction, we introduce five nested conditions and show every cone falls into one of the six classes exactly. The first four classes are proved and described to be nonempty, but the last two still remain some possibilities for their existence. The conditions are shaped by relative infinitesimals, the pairs of ring and ideal, and the leading coefficients. However, some of the types have no example and are unknown for the existence of the lattice order. The Birkhoff-Pierce problem still remains open in this paper.

Section 2 includes the necessary concepts and terms that ones need to know for the paper. Section 3 constructs the Puiseux expansion of complex numbers and the basic orders, proving the basic orders. Section 4 defines the six types of the stratification of the directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C, demonstrating the Covering Lemma and explaining each type of directed partial order.

#

The purpose of this section is to mention some concepts and notations that appear in the proofs. For a subset III of C\mathbb{C}C, we write I×=I∖{0}I^{\times} = I \setminus \{0\}I×=I∖{0}. We define i=−1i = \sqrt{-1}i=−1​.

Let K⊆LK \subseteq LK⊆L be fields. We use two standard facts: the set of elements of an algebraically closed field that are algebraic over a given subfield is an algebraically closed subfield; if LLL is algebraic over KKK, then every embedding of KKK into an algebraically closed field extends to an embedding of LLL. When we decide the variable and the coefficients, three things guarantees the choice. First, the variable ttt must be transcendental over the field FFF of coefficients. Second, FFF must be algebraically closed because of the Newton-Puiseux Theorem 2.1. Third, FFF must be large enough in order that every complex number is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t) in order to let C\mathbb{C}C inside the series field. A transcendence basis TTT is the tool to achieve them at the same time. We fix a transcendence basis TTT of C\mathbb{C}C over Q\mathbb{Q}Q and one element t∈Tt \in Tt∈T. 3. Complex Numbers with Puiseux Series
#

In this section, we rewrite every complex number as the form of series and construct the basic directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C. There are three steps: we isolate one transcendental number ttt, embed C\mathbb{C}C into a field of Puiseux series in s=1ts = \frac{1}{t}s=t1​, and define positivity by a condition on the first coefficient.

Definition 3.1. The field of Puiseux series over kkk in sss is

k{{s}}=⋃n≥1k((s1/n)). k\{\{s\}\} = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} k\big((s^{1/n})\big). k{{s}}=n≥1⋃​k((s1/n)).

Thus, a nonzero Puiseux series is a formal sum ∑qcqsq\sum_q c_q s^q∑q​cq​sq with cq∈kc_q \in kcq​∈k, whose exponents qqq are rational numbers with a common denominator and are bounded below. Fractional exponents cannot be avoided. A square root of sss is not a Laurent series in sss.

Lemma 3.1. There is an embedding of fields ι:C→F{{s}}\iota: \mathbb{C} \to F\{\{s\}\}ι:C→F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1.

Proof. The set of elements of C\mathbb{C}C that are algebraic over a subfield is an algebraically closed subfield, and it contains every number algebraic over Q\mathbb{Q}Q. If ttt were algebraic over FFF, it would be algebraic over Q(T∖{t})\mathbb{Q}(T \setminus \{t\})Q(T∖{t}), contradicting the algebraic independence of TTT. Thus, FFF which contains Q‾\overline{\mathbb{Q}}Q​ is an algebraically closed subfield of C\mathbb{C}C, and ttt is transcendental over FFF. Therefore, there is an isomorphism of F(t)F(t)F(t) onto the subfield F(s)F(s)F(s) of F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} which is the identity on FFF and sends ttt to s−1s^{-1}s−1. By Theorem 2.1, the field F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}} is algebraically closed. Because every complex number is algebraic over Q(T)\mathbb{Q}(T)Q(T) and Q(T)⊆F(t)\mathbb{Q}(T) \subseteq F(t)Q(T)⊆F(t), every complex number is algebraic over F(t)=F(s)F(t) = F(s)F(t)=F(s). Hence, C\mathbb{C}C is algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t). Thus, the isomorphism generalizes to an embedding of C\mathbb{C}C. □\square□

3.1 The Expansion
#

Now, C\mathbb{C}C and the field of Puiseux series are two different objects. An order defined by “the first coefficient” needs every complex number to be a series. The embedding of Lemma 3.1 provides that it is a dictionary to translate each complex number into a series without changing sums and products. After the translation, the cone conditions become the statements about adding and multiplying series.

We fix an embedding ι\iotaι as the one in Lemma 3.1 and identify a complex number zzz with the series ι(z)\iota(z)ι(z). Thus, every nonzero z∈Cz \in \mathbb{C}z∈C has an expansion

z=∑qzqsq,zq∈F. z = \sum_q z_q s^q, \qquad z_q \in F. z=q∑​zq​sq,zq​∈F.

It is like a decimal expansion. The image of C\mathbb{C}C is an algebraically closed field containing FFF and sss, so, for every n≥1n \ge 1n≥1, it contains all nnn roots of the polynomial xn−sx^n - sxn−s existing in F{{s}}F\{\{s\}\}F{{s}}. The series s1/ns^{1/n}s1/n is one of them. Thus, sqs^qsq and tqt^qtq are complex numbers for every rational number qqq.

Example 1. Let zzz be a complex number with z2=t2+tz^2 = t^2 + tz2=t2+t. Only algebraic over F(t)F(t)F(t), it is not a rational function of ttt. Writing t2+t=t2(1+s)t^2 + t = t^2(1 + s)t2+t=t2(1+s) and expanding the square root by the binomial series gives

z=s−1(1+s)1/2=s−1+12−18s+⋯ . z = s^{-1}(1+s)^{1/2} = s^{-1} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{8}s + \cdots. z=s−1(1+s)1/2=s−1+21​−81​s+⋯.

Thus, zzz has the size of s−1=ts^{-1} = ts−1=t and the first coefficient 111. An order reading the first term only calls zzz positive. The other solution −z-z−z has the series −s−1−12+⋯-s^{-1} - \frac{1}{2} + \cdots−s−1−21​+⋯, with first coefficient −1-1−1. Decided by the embedding ι\iotaι, ttt determines which solution begins with +s−1+s^{-1}+s−1.

Another simple example is a square root of ttt, which is s−12s^{-\frac{1}{2}}s−21​, explaining why fraction exponents are needed.

The expansion is the way of writing the number in order that the orders below can read its coefficients. By the axiom of choice, it depends on the choice of TTT and of the embedding ι\iotaι. We know no directed partial order on C\mathbb{C}C is defined without this choice.

3.2 Level, Leading Coefficient, and Normalized Series
#

A rule reading the beginning of a series observes the things of the place where the series begins and with which coefficient. The first one is defined as the level which measures the size of the number and replaces the absolute value. It is useless here because it does not come from an order on C\mathbb{C}C. The second one is the leading coefficient.

Definition 3.2. Let z∈Cz \in \mathbb{C}z∈C be nonzero.

  1. The level lev⁡(z)\operatorname{lev}(z)lev(z) is the smallest exponent qqq with zq≠0z_q \ne 0zq​=0.

  3. The normalized series is u=z/slev⁡(z)=∑r≥0ursru = z/s^{\operatorname{lev}(z)} = \sum_{r \ge 0} u_r s^ru=z/slev(z)=∑r≥0​ur​sr, so u0=lc⁡(z)u_0 = \operatorname{lc}(z)u0​=lc(z).

The property is obtained directly from the definition: lev⁡(c)=0\operatorname{lev}(c) = 0lev(c)=0, lc⁡(c)=c\operatorname{lc}(c) = clc(c)=c for c∈F×c \in F^{\times}c∈F×; lev⁡(sq)=q\operatorname{lev}(s^q) = qlev(sq)=q, lc⁡(sq)=1\operatorname{lc}(s^q) = 1lc(sq)=1 for q∈Qq \in \mathbb{Q}q∈Q; lc⁡(−z)=−lc⁡(z)\operatorname{lc}(-z) = -\operatorname{lc}(z)lc(−z)=−lc(z). The normalized series removes the size, so the numbers of different sizes can be compared digit by digit. To be noticed, a very negative level implies a very large number due to s−1=ts^{-1} = ts−1=t. For instance, in Example 1, the level is −1-1−1; the leading coefficient is 111; the normalized series is (1+s)1/2=1+12s−18s2+⋯(1+s)^{1/2} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}s - \frac{1}{8}s^2 + \cdots(1+s)1/2=1+21​s−81​s2+⋯.

Lemma 3.2. The level is a valuation on C\mathbb{C}C with value group Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

lev⁡(zw)=lev⁡(z)+lev⁡(w),lev⁡(z+w)≥min⁡{lev⁡(z),lev⁡(w)}. \operatorname{lev}(zw) = \operatorname{lev}(z) + \operatorname{lev}(w), \qquad \operatorname{lev}(z+w) \ge \min\{\operatorname{lev}(z), \operatorname{lev}(w)\}. lev(zw)=lev(z)+lev(w),lev(z+w)≥min{lev(z),lev(w)}.

If q=q′q = q'q=q′, then z+w=sq((a+b)+⋯ )z + w = s^q((a+b) + \cdots)z+w=sq((a+b)+⋯), which has level qqq and leading coefficient a+ba+ba+b when a+b≠0a+b \ne 0a+b=0. Lemma 3.2 explains how the two data are the right ones. Under multiplication and addition, they change in a predictable way, and this is all to verify the cone conditions. Furthermore, we write O\mathcal{O}O for the ring of numbers of level ≥0\ge 0≥0 (together with 000), m\mathfrak{m}m for the ideal of numbers of level greater than 000, and IδI_{\delta}Iδ​ for the ideal of numbers of level greater than δ\deltaδ.

3.3 The Basic Order by the First Coefficient
#

We call zzz positive when its leading coefficient is positive. However, the leading coefficient lies in FFF which contains iii and has no total order, so the word “positive” has no actual meaning yet. The necessary thing is a set SSS of admissible leading coefficients, and the conditions on SSS are dictated by the cone conditions for C\mathbb{C}C. The set SSS must be closed under multiplication and addition. The first terms cannot be canceled by the condition S∩(−S)={0}S \cap (-S) = \{0\}S∩(−S)={0}. These are exactly the conditions for a cone on FFF. Thus, a cone on the small field FFF becomes to a cone on C\mathbb{C}C.

Theorem 3.3. The Birkhoff-Pierce problem asks for a lattice order, so the first question about the new order is whether it is the one. The natural pair usually for testing is 000 and iii, because these two numbers are incomparable on C\mathbb{C}C that is proved in Lemma 2.2. The idea of the test is that an upper bound of 000 and iii must be a “large” number (of negative level). However, among large numbers, there is no the smallest one because from any large number one can subtract a number that is still large, and the result is an upper bound. The following lemma and theorem demonstrate the idea more clearly.

4. The Stratification on the Complex Field
#

Section 3 produced some examples by the expansion of complex numbers with the Puiseux series. In this section, we attempt to stratify all the directed partial order in C\mathbb{C}C, including those not given by any series. Therefore, we need a property valid for an arbitrary cone and separating the orders we know. The proof of Theorem 3.6 suggests such a property. The basic orders fail to be lattice orders because a positive number still stays positive when it is changed a little, causing an upper bound can always be lowered a little. A lattice order must behave differently when it exists. Hence, we stratify the orders by their sensitivity to small changes.

4.1 Windows
#

The basic orders read one term of the series. To find more orders and stratify them, we let a rule read a longer piece by inducing the definition of the window in order to make “the first few terms” clear. The window is dependent on the normalized series, so its width is measured from the first term of each number and not from a fixed exponent, allowing the windows to be compatible with multiplication. Because the width δ\deltaδ is fixed, the rule reads the same amount of every number.

4.2 Rules and Small Change
#

Let PPP be a cone on C\mathbb{C}C. For the basic order D=d(Q≥0)D = d(\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0})D=d(Q≥0​) in Theorem 3.3, a number is positive when its leading coefficient is a positive rational number. The classification is built on the observation that an order is described by the small changes z↦z(1+ε)z \mapsto z(1+\varepsilon)z↦z(1+ε) which can never destruct positivity. The word “small” means that it is specified by a pair.

For an arbitrary cone with no given expansion, we need a notion of smallness using only in the field operations. A set a\mathfrak{a}a of small numbers should have two properties that the sum of two small numbers is small and a small number times a moderate number is small. If RRR denotes the set of moderate numbers, this illustrates that a\mathfrak{a}a is an ideal of the ring RRR. We ask that the quotient field of RRR is C\mathbb{C}C so that any two complex numbers can be compared through a quotient r1/r2r_1/r_2r1​/r2​ of elements of RRR, allowing one small change to act on two positive numbers at the same time. The change is multiplicative z↦z(1+a)z \mapsto z(1+\mathfrak{a})z↦z(1+a) but not additive z↦z+az \mapsto z + \mathfrak{a}z↦z+a because smallness is relative to the size of zzz.

4.3 The Five Conditions
#

From Section 3, we know that smallness is measured by a series expansion with a valuation, and positivity depends only on the first term or on a window. In this subsection, each condition is obtained from the previous one by giving up one requirement.

Definition 4.3. For a cone PPP, let I(P)I(P)I(P) be the set of all ε∈C\varepsilon \in \mathbb{C}ε∈C such that z(1+nε)∈Pz(1 + n\varepsilon) \in Pz(1+nε)∈P for some z∈P×z \in P^{\times}z∈P× and all n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z.

Definition 4.4 (The five conditions). For a cone P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} on C\mathbb{C}C:

  1. AAA: P=P[mw]P = P[\mathfrak{m}_w]P=P[mw​] for some nontrivial valuation www of C\mathbb{C}C.
  2. BBB: P=P[Iδw]P = P[I^{w}_{\delta}]P=P[Iδw​] for some nontrivial valuation www of C\mathbb{C}C and some δ≥0\delta \ge 0δ≥0.
  3. CCC: P=P[a]P = P[\mathfrak{a}]P=P[a] for some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a).
  4. DDD: P[a]≠{0}P[\mathfrak{a}] \ne \{0\}P[a]={0} for some pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a).
  5. EEE: I(P)≠{0}I(P) \ne \{0\}I(P)={0}.

The condition AAA is for the series expansion whose positivity depends only on the first term. The condition BBB is for the series expansion whose positivity depends only on a window of fixed width. The condition CCC indicates that small changes cannot destruct positivity, for some notion of small. The condition DDD is that they cannot destruct the positivity of at least one number. Condition EEE says that there are relative infinitesimals; its failure corresponds to the Archimedean case.

Definition 4.5 (The six types). A directed partial order PPP on C\mathbb{C}C is of

  • Type 1 if AAA holds (the rule reads only the first term of some series expansion);
  • Type 2 if BBB holds but AAA does not (the rule reads a window of fixed width);
  • Type 3 if CCC holds but BBB does not (for some pair all positive numbers are insensitive to the small changes, but positivity is not described by a window of one valuation);
  • Type 4 if DDD holds but CCC does not (some positive number is insensitive to the small changes, but no single pair makes all positive numbers insensitive);
  • Type 5 if EEE holds but DDD does not (there are infinitely small elements, but every positive number is sensitive to arbitrarily small changes);
  • Type 6 if EEE does not hold (there are no infinitely small elements).

A stratification must achieve the goal that every order is placed in exactly one class. We obtain it because the five conditions are nested. To decide their type, every cone has a condition it satisfies, or satisfies nothing. The proof of their covering is in the rest of this subsection.

Lemma 4.3. For every cone P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} on C\mathbb{C}C,

A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E. A \Rightarrow B \Rightarrow C \Rightarrow D \Rightarrow E. A⇒B⇒C⇒D⇒E.

Proof. A⇒BA \Rightarrow BA⇒B: take δ=0\delta = 0δ=0, since I0w=mwI^{w}_{0} = \mathfrak{m}_wI0w​=mw​.

B⇒CB \Rightarrow CB⇒C: (Ow,Iδw)(\mathcal{O}_w, I^{w}_{\delta})(Ow​,Iδw​) is a pair by Lemma 2.4.

C⇒DC \Rightarrow DC⇒D: P[a]=P≠{0}P[\mathfrak{a}] = P \ne \{0\}P[a]=P={0}.

D⇒ED \Rightarrow ED⇒E: let z∈P[a]z \in P[\mathfrak{a}]z∈P[a] and ε∈a\varepsilon \in \mathfrak{a}ε∈a be nonzero. For every n∈Zn \in \mathbb{Z}n∈Z, we have nε∈an\varepsilon \in \mathfrak{a}nε∈a, so z(1+nε)∈Pz(1+n\varepsilon) \in Pz(1+nε)∈P. Hence ε∈I(P)\varepsilon \in I(P)ε∈I(P). □\square□

Theorem 4.4 (Covering Lemma). For P≠0P \ne 0P=0, every directed partial order on C\mathbb{C}C is of exactly one of the Types 1 to 6.

Proof. Let PPP be a directed partial order. Then P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0}. By Lemma 4.3, if one of the conditions holds, then all later ones hold. Thus, the set of conditions that hold for PPP is one of {A,…,E}\{A, \dots, E\}{A,…,E}, {B,…,E}\{B, \dots, E\}{B,…,E}, {C,D,E}\{C, D, E\}{C,D,E}, {D,E}\{D, E\}{D,E}, {E}\{E\}{E}, ∅\emptyset∅. These six cases exclude each other and are the types 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of Definition 4.5 in this order. □\square□

4.4 The Six Types
#

The Covering Lemma holds for the nested conditions, so an order is classified by the first condition it satisfies. The rest of this section explains the types one by one. Types 1 and 2 are described in details; Types 3 and 4 are demonstrated by constructions with examples; Types 5 and 6 are shown by stating what is known because it has not been explored adequately yet.

Type 2
#

The next rule reads a fixed number of more terms which is determined by a window. In Type 1, for each level, windows are admissible, and this table is called a card. The question is which cards define orders. There are another two conditions of the direct translations that the product and the sum of positive numbers are positive by windows.

A cone PPP has depth at most δ\deltaδ if P=P[Iδ]P = P[I_{\delta}]P=P[Iδ​]. By Lemma 4.1, this means that positivity depends only on the level and the window of width δ\deltaδ.

Type 4
#

In Types 1–3, every positive number is insensitive to small changes for some pair. Type 4 consists of orders in which this fails for at least one positive number: small changes do not matter all the time. To build one, we stick two opposite parts. For large numbers (of negative level), we keep the first-term rule, which is insensitive. At level 000, we put a rigid set where no change is allowed; the natural numbers N\mathbb{N}N are the apparent choice by being closed under addition and multiplication and having gaps between their elements. The two parts can fit together.

Thus, Type 6 consists of the directed partial orders with no nonzero relative infinitesimal. Type 5 consists of the orders having relative infinitesimals where, for every pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a), every positive number loses its positivity under some change z↦z(1+a)z \mapsto z(1+a)z↦z(1+a), a∈aa \in \mathfrak{a}a∈a.

Does C\mathbb{C}C have a directed partial order of Type 5 or 6? We know no construction of an order of either type and cannot prove that none exists. All directed partial orders on C\mathbb{C}C constructed in this paper are belonged to Types 1 to 4, and we have not determined the types of the orders of [2, 9].

4.5 Lattice orders
#

We return to the original question of Birkhoff-Pierce problem. In Theorem 3.6, the supremum of 000 and iii failed to exist because an upper bound could be lowered by a number small compared with it with using the expansion. The wiggle Lemma 2.3 isolates what a supremum that a single nonzero change ddd can be added to and subtracted from both differences h−xh - xh−x and h−yh - yh−y. Condition CCC always provides such ddd by Lemma 4.2, so it works for every pair without any expansion.

Theorem 4.13. Let P≠{0}P \ne \{0\}P={0} be a cone on C\mathbb{C}C satisfying condition CCC. Then two complex numbers have a supremum for PPP only if they are comparable, and PPP is not a lattice order.

Proof. Let P=P[a]P = P[\mathfrak{a}]P=P[a] for a pair (R,a)(R, \mathfrak{a})(R,a). Suppose x,yx, yx,y are incomparable and h=x∨yh = x \vee yh=x∨y exists. By Lemma 2.3, p=h−xp = h - xp=h−x and q=h−yq = h - yq=h−y are positive and [−p,p]∩[−q,q]={0}[-p, p] \cap [-q, q] = \{0\}[−p,p]∩[−q,q]={0}. However, Lemma 4.2 gives a nonzero ddd in this intersection, so no two incomparable numbers have a supremum. By Lemma 2.2, for p∈P×p \in P^{\times}p∈P×, the numbers 000 and ipipip are incomparable, so PPP is not a lattice order. Types 1, 2 and 3 satisfy condition CCC by Lemma 4.3. □\square□

When small changes do not matter anymore, any upper bound of two incomparable numbers can be lowered a little and still be an upper bound, so there is no least one. This is the core of Theorem 3.6, where the upper bound hhh of 000 and iii was lowered by ta2t^{\frac{a}{2}}t2a​. Theorem 4.13 needs no hypothesis on the set SSS of the first coefficients. The order HHH of Type 4 is not a lattice order either by Theorem 4.11. We attempt to stratify all the directed partial orders on the complex field, but the question of the existence of lattice order is still remained open.
